0.why: On a server never updated since install, any hash change is suspicious, and the key treats the earliest iptables-save entry as the start; that entry is really only the baseline.

whyNot.A: The /etc/passwd hash changes on 1/1 come after the iptables-save hash changed on 12/31, so they are not the first.
whyNot.C: The key rejects this, though it is the first entry where the iptables-save hash differs from the baseline.
whyNot.D: The initrd.img hash change on 1/1 at 3:30 is the latest change in the log, so it cannot be first.

0.keyDoubt: C, because the iptables-save hash first changes from ...cc3 to ...co3 at 12/31 2:00, while the 12/30 entry is just the baseline.

1.why: Screen lock is a mobile device hardening control that prevents unauthorized access to a lost or unattended company-managed smartphone.

whyNot.B: Terminal servers sit in controlled data centers and are not locked by idle-screen timers in the same way as handheld devices.

2.why: A strong password or PIN is a core mobile device management control that protects a company-managed smartphone against unauthorized access.

whyNot.B: Data center servers rely mainly on physical and network controls, and this simulation pairs strong passwords with the phone.

3.why: Device encryption protects data at rest on a portable smartphone that can be lost or stolen, a standard mobile device management requirement.

whyNot.B: A server in a physically secured data center is not the intended match for this device-level, loss-driven control.

4.why: Remote wipe lets administrators erase corporate data from a lost or stolen mobile device, a classic mobile device management capability.

whyNot.B: Servers in a data center are not lost or stolen in the field, so remote wipe is not their typical control.

5.why: GPS tracking locates a lost or stolen mobile device, so it applies to the portable company-managed smartphone.

whyNot.B: A fixed data center server has a known location and does not need GPS tracking.

6.why: A pop-up blocker is a browser-level control on a smartphone used for web browsing, reducing malicious ads and drive-by content.

7.why: Cable locks are a physical security control that deters theft of hardware, matching the data center terminal server in this exercise.

8.why: Antivirus is an endpoint protection control that detects malware on servers, so it belongs with the data center terminal server.

9.why: A host-based firewall filters traffic on an individual server, providing a host-level network control for the data center terminal server.

10.why: A proximity reader is a physical access control that restricts entry to the data center where the terminal server is housed.

11.why: A sniffer (protocol analyzer) is used to monitor and analyze traffic on the data center network where the terminal server sits.

22.why: RAID-0 striping maximizes read and write throughput, which suits streaming media where speed matters and redundancy does not.

whyNot.B: RAID-1 mirroring prioritizes redundancy and halves usable capacity, which streaming does not need.
whyNot.C: RAID-5 parity adds write overhead and redundancy that this workload does not need.
whyNot.D: RAID-6 uses two parity blocks, adding overhead and cost that streaming does not justify.

23.why: RAID-1 mirroring keeps an exact copy of the data, giving simple, reliable fault tolerance for a small, critical authentication server.

whyNot.A: RAID-0 has no redundancy, so one disk failure would take authentication down.
whyNot.C: RAID-5 is better suited to larger, read-heavy arrays than a small authentication volume.
whyNot.D: RAID-6 needs more disks and has more overhead than this server needs.

24.why: RAID-5 stripes data with single parity, balancing capacity, read performance and tolerance of one disk failure, which suits an archive.

whyNot.A: RAID-0 offers no fault tolerance, which is unacceptable for archived mail.
whyNot.B: RAID-1 wastes half the capacity, which is costly for a large archive.
whyNot.D: RAID-6 survives two failures but costs more capacity than an archive needs.

25.why: RAID-6 uses double parity and survives two simultaneous disk failures, fitting a critical identity management system.

whyNot.A: RAID-0 has no redundancy and would risk losing identity data.
whyNot.B: RAID-1 tolerates only one disk failure in the mirrored pair and offers less capacity efficiency.
whyNot.C: RAID-5 survives only one disk failure, which is less resilient than RAID-6.

26.why: RAID-5 stripes data across the disks with distributed single parity, so 4 disks give 3 disks of data capacity plus 1 of parity.

whyNot.B: Mirroring with no parity describes RAID-1, not RAID-5.
whyNot.C: Two parity boxes describe RAID-6, and 4 data plus 2 parity cannot fit on 4 disks.
whyNot.D: Striping with no parity describes RAID-0, which has no redundancy.

27.why: RAID-6 stripes data with two parity blocks, so the build is striping plus both parity boxes checked, tolerating two disk failures.

whyNot.A: One parity box describes RAID-5, not RAID-6.
whyNot.B: Mirroring with no parity describes RAID-1.
whyNot.D: Striping with no parity describes RAID-0.

34.why: CPU cache and registers are the most volatile data, lost almost instantly and changing constantly, so they are collected first in the order of volatility.

whyNot.B: RAM is less volatile than CPU cache and comes second.
whyNot.C: Swap space is on disk and is less volatile than RAM.
whyNot.D: Hard drive data persists without power and is among the least volatile.

35.why: RAM holds running processes, network connections, and keys, and is lost at power-off. It is the second most volatile source after CPU cache.

whyNot.A: CPU cache is more volatile and ranks first.
whyNot.C: Swap is disk-backed and persists longer than RAM.
whyNot.D: Hard drive data is non-volatile and ranks after swap.

36.why: Swap or page-file data lives on disk but is tied to the running system and is often overwritten or cleared, so it ranks third.

whyNot.A: CPU cache is the most volatile, not third.
whyNot.B: RAM is more volatile than swap and ranks second.
whyNot.D: The hard drive's persistent data is the least volatile of these.

37.why: Data on a hard drive persists without power, so it is the least volatile of these and collected last.

whyNot.A: CPU cache is the most volatile item.
whyNot.B: RAM loses its contents at power-off, so it ranks much higher.
whyNot.C: Swap is more volatile than general disk contents.

whyNot.C: Multi-factor needs two or more factor categories, and a password is only one.
